name: Wall sit
summary: Quad endurance against a wall, at a depth your knees are happy with.
setup: Camera side-on, 2–3 m away, roughly hip height. Back flat on the wall, feet a good step out from it, shoulder-width apart. Slide down to a comfortable depth — thighs level is the classic target, a shallower bend if the kneecap complains. Whole body in frame.
brief: Back flat on the wall, feet a good step out from it, shoulder-width apart. Slide down to a comfortable depth and hold it there.
why: From the side the camera reads knee angle and whether your shins are vertical (knees not past toes) — both invisible from the front.

guide.surface: A flat wall with nothing on it and a non-slip floor. Barefoot or grippy shoes.

points.t: Feet hip- to shoulder-width apart, toes pointing straight ahead, both feet flat with weight spread across the whole foot — heels stay down.
Feet far enough from the wall that when you slide down the shins are vertical and the knees sit directly above the ankles — usually about 50 cm.
Knees bent to 90°: thighs parallel to the floor, shins vertical.
Knees track in line with the second toe — not falling inward toward each other, not pushed out. (Facing the camera side-on, the coach cannot see this; check it yourself in a mirror once.)
Knees do not travel forward past the toes.
Hips at the same height as the knees, pressed back into the wall. Pelvis neutral — a small gap at the lower back is normal.
Whole back — sacrum, mid-back and shoulder blades — in contact with the wall. Do not let the upper body lean forward off it.
Shoulders relaxed and back against the wall. Arms hanging at your sides, crossed over the chest, or held straight out in front — never resting on the thighs, which unloads the quads.
Back of the head touching the wall, chin level, eyes forward.
Breathe steadily throughout; do not hold your breath as it burns. The hold ends when the knee angle or the back on the wall gives way, not when you decide to push through.

guide.stop: Pain builds behind or around the kneecap (a burn in the front of the thigh is expected; kneecap pain is not).

enterCue: Slide down the wall until your knees are at ninety
tempo: Slide down over 2 s, hold, stand up over 2 s.
progression: Longer holds; a weight on the thighs.
regression: Shallower knee bend (much easier on the kneecap), shorter holds.
contraindications: Kneecap pain. Around 90° is where the kneecap is loaded most, so start shallower — a quarter or half bend — and deepen only if it stays comfortable.

faults.label: Sitting too high
faults.tip: Thighs parallel is the classic target. Sitting higher than that is fine and easier on the kneecap — it is the hold time that builds the quad.

faults.label: Below 90°
faults.cue: Come up a touch — knees at ninety
faults.tip: Compression behind the kneecap is greatest around a right angle, and grows as you go deeper still. If the kneecap complains, sit higher rather than lower.

faults.label: Back off the wall
faults.cue: Press your back into the wall
faults.tip: Shoulder blades, mid-back and hips all stay on the wall; leaning forward shifts load to the knees.

faults.label: Knees past toes
faults.cue: Walk your feet out — shins vertical
faults.tip: Keep the shin vertical so the load stays in the quads, not the kneecap.

faults.label: Hands resting on thighs
faults.tip: Arms at your sides, crossed, or out in front — resting on the thighs takes load off the quads.

faults.label: Heel lifting
faults.tip: Feet flat, a good step from the wall; if the heels lift, walk the feet out a little.
